MOB NEEDS ONLY LEADER MAY CARRY OUT THREAT TO STORM JAIL. Seek Life of Negro Charged With Assault Upon Young White Girl. Excited Crowds Throng Streets.
Amory, Miss., Aug. 29—Excited crowds marched the streets of Amory tonight threatening vengeance to a negro, identity unknown, who, it is charged, assaulted a young white woman several days ago, and apparently are awaiting only the appearance of a leader to put into execution a threat to storm the county jail where the man is held.

The negro, it is alleged, attacked the 17-year-old daughter of William Jackson, a planter, as she was passing through a thicket, returning from a visit to a neighboring plantation near Amory late Saturday evening. Her condition is reported as serious.

The man escaped but was pursued and captured by a Sheriff's posse in a barn near the scene of the crime this afternoon and was hurried to prison, where a strong guard was established in anticipation of the forming of a mob. The crowds came immediately with the spreading of the news about the countryside of his arrest, but at a late hour had made no effort to put their threats of lynching into effect.
amory-amory-1910-08-29.A6:
AMORY MOB CLAMORS FOR LIFE OF A NEGRO
Starkville, Miss., Aug. 30.—With a thousand men surrounding Stockton's stables at Amory, clamoring for the life of a negro concealed in a stall, it is probable his life will be forfeited at the stake, for alleged brutal assault on the seevnteen-year-old daughter of William Jackson, a prominent farmer four miles from Amory.

Officers and the best citizens are exerting every effort to stay the mob, but to no avail. The girl is in a critical condition and her recovery is doubtful.

Negro Proves Innocence. Amory, Miss., Aug. 30.—Proving that he was not the man wanted for the assault upon a 16-year-old daughter of a farmer near here, the negro, who was last night threatened with lynching by a mob which had collected in the neighborhood of the jail, was released today. Three other negrces who have been arrested were brought here today for identification by the young woman. Officers believe that one of them committed the assault. The town is still thronged with people and excitement is running high But Many Tired, Rheumatic, Nervous People Don't Know How to Find It. COUNTY FAIR FOR MOBILE PLANS LAID BY BUSINESS MEN OF GULF CITY. Institution Will Inaugurate New Feature in Oyster Exhibit, Showing Natural Resources of Alabama's Sea Coast.
Mobile, Aug. 30.—(Special.)—After a lapse of many years Mobile is to have a county fair. It will be on an clab- orate scale and will be held at Monroe Park after the present summer season. The fair will be under the auspices of the Mobile Commercial Club and the membership of the several committees include some of the most prominent men of the city and county. Already declarations have been received from many farmers and truck growers of their intention to make exhibits of the products of the soil of the county and all the manufacturing companies in the city and county will place their wares on exhibit.

One of the most unique exhibits and the first of the kind in the South will be an oyster exhibition under the auspices of the Alabama Oyster Commission. It is proposed in this exhibit to show all the different varieties of oysters grown in Alabama waters, have shuckers and packers on hand to show how the oysters are opened and prepared for shipping in the raw state and in cans.

MOB TAKES LAW IN HAND LYNCHED NEGRO WHO ASSAULTED WHITE GIRL. Two Thousand Persons Participate in Affair in Mississippi Town—Mob Disperses as Quickly as it Forms.
Amory, Miss., Sept. 1.—Nick Thompson, a negro, accused of criminally assaulting a 17-year-old girl at Jackson Crossing, near here, last Saturday, was taken to the scene of the crime this afternoon by a mob and lynched. Fully 2,000 persons participated in the lynching.

The lynching followed the identification of Thompson by Miss Jennie Jackson, his alleged victim. As soon as the fact that the negro had been identified became known, the mob quickly formed and hanged him to a telegraph pole. After accomplishing its purpose, the mob dispersed.

Miss Jackson was attacked Saturday afternoon while returning home from a neighbor's.

Six negroes besides Thompson were arrested on suspicion, but were later released after proving alibis. Intense excitement reigned following the attack, and only the intervention of cooler heads prevented a lynching when the first arrests were made.

NEGRO LYNCHEO BY MOB
ACCUSED OF ASSAULTING THE DAUGHTER OF A WELTHY PLANTER.
After Swinging a Minute He Was Lowered and Asked to Confess—Refusing He was Executed.
United Press Special.
Amory, Miss., Sept 2. — Nick Thompson, colored, was lynched here last night for assaulting the seven-year-old daughter of William Jackson, a wealthy planter. Thompson refused to confess when the mob lowered him after he had been hanging one minute. He was jerked up again and allowed to hang until he was dead. Two thousand citizens, friends of Jackson, dragged Thompson from the jail last night.
amory-amory-1910-08-29.A14:
Atrocious Assault.
An atrocious assault was made on Miss Jennie Jackson, the 17 year old daughter of Mr. W. L. Jackson, at Jackson crossing last Saturday evening. The assault was made by a brutal negro, who had concealed himself in the underbrush and assaulted the young lady as she was returning from the house of a neighbor near her home. The alarm was given and dogs from New Albany were put on his trail. Several negroes have been arrested and held under suspicion, but identification of the right one has not been fully made up to this time. The whole country has turned out in pursuit and if the fiend is found and identified will be sent by the rope route to death.

henry-cox-raggio-1910-08-28.A1:
DANCE ENDS IN QUARREL TWO KILLED, FOUR BADLY WOUNDED. White Man Orders Negro to Cense Al- tercation With Wife—Latter Refuses and Gun Play Follows.
Marianna, Ark., Aug. 28—Two negroes were killed, three were wounded and a white man was fatally injured in a fight which originated in a dance hall quarrel at Raggio, twelve miles east of here, last night. The battle occurred about 1 o'clock this morning.

News of the battle was brought to Marianna at daybreak this morning by a negro wh came to purchase coffins. The dead are Mack Harvey and Henry Cox. The wounded negroes are Eli Davis, Pleas Bailey, and Dault Marchbanks. John Russell, a white man, is said to be dying.

According to the story brought by the negro, a dance was in progress when an altercation arose between Mack Harvey and his wife. Russell, the white man, ordered them to cease quarrelling. Harvey turned on the white man and declared he would talk to his wife any way he pleased. Russell left and returned shortly with two other white men. In the meantime Harvey secured friends and awaited the return of the white men. The negro message bearer was too frightened to give a coherent story of the shooting which followed.

Sheriff Ford returned to Marianna late this evening and reported the arrest of half a dozen negroes. He said the men whom Russell secured to aid him were deputy constables and that the shooting was precipitated when Harvey refused to be placed under arrest.

More than fifty shots were exchanged in the battle. Four of the negroes under arrest are wounded, one of them probably fatally. High excitement prevails, though no immediate outbreak is anticipated.
henry-cox-raggio-1910-08-28.A2:
PEACEMAKER LOSES LIFE.
Shot While Trying to End Domestic
Quarrel at a Dance.
MARIANNA, Ark., August 20. — Two negroes were killed and three others injured, while John Russell, a white man, was fatally shot at a dance at Raggio yesterday. News of the fight reached Marianna last night, when a negro came for coffins. Russell attempted to end a quarrel between Mack Harvey and his wife. Russell left the dance hall, and when he returned with two officers to arrest Harvey, Harvey started shooting. More than fifty shots were fired.

john-wayne-hinton-1910-08-16.A6:
POSSES HUNT NEGRO TO AVENGE CRIME
Bride Is Assaulted and Beheaded After Husband Is Laid Out.
CHARLESTON, W. Va., Aug. 16.—Mining towns in this section are wrought up to a high pitch over the assault and murder of Mrs. John Alliff by a negro, who also murderously assaulted her husband, leaving him for dead after taking his valuables.

Three suspects are under arrest in nearby towns and lynchings are feared.

The crime was committed Sunday night near Quinnemont. Alliff and his bride of three weeks were walking alor; the Chesapeake and Ohio railway tracks on their way from the home of the young woman's mother, when the negro sprang from behind a boulder and knocked him senseless with an iron bar.

Leaving the husband for dead, the negro attacked Mrs. Alliff, afterward severing her head from the body. The mutilated body was thrown into Laurel creek.

Section men found Alliff beside the track and he was taken to Hinton on a special train and is in a critical condition, ignorant of the terrible fate of his wife, for whom he calls in moments when he is conscious.

The aged mother of Mrs. Alliff collapsed when she saw the mutilated body of her daughter in the morgue and is also in a critical condition because of the shock.

Fayette county has offered a reward of $500 for the capture of the negro and the Chesapeake and Ohio railway has also offered a reward, Alliff being a brakeman.

Posses of enraged men, with rifles and bloodhounds, are scouring the mountains near the scene of the crime. Despite the arrest of the three suspects. Every effort is being put forth to capture the flendish assailant.

TROOPS GUARD NEGRO.
Mob Wanted to Lynch him and Martial Law enforced in town. By United Press Leased Special Wire
Mob Wanted to Lynch him and Martial Law enforced in town.
By United Press Leased Special Wire, HINTON, W. Va., Aug. 17.—Three companies of militia arrived here today to prevent the Lynching of John Wayne, a negro, accused of assaulting and killing Mrs. John Ailliss and beating her husband, whose death is hourly expected.
Following the negro's escape yesterday from a mob of 1,000 infuriated citizens, the negro was taken to the woods by the officers and whereabouts today are unknown. It is, however, believed that he has bee quietly placed in jail in some of the neighboring towns. Because of Ailliss' condition he was unable to identify the negro Four companies of militia are now here and the town is under martial rule.
john-wayne-hinton-1910-08-16.A9:
MOB GATHERED TO HANG BRUTE ARRESTED ON CHARGE OF MURDER—HE WAS SPIRITED AWAY TO THE MOUNTAINS AND A LYNCHING AVERTED BY THIS ACTION.
BLOOD IS FOUND ON CLOTHES
QUICK WORK OF OFFICERS AND CARE IN GUARDING PRISONER ALL THAT KEPT SUMMERS COUNTY FROM BEING SCENE OF LYNCHING.
HINTON, W. Va., Aug. 17.—After an afternoon and night of conflict between troops, officers and citizens on one side and a determined mob on the other, Thomas Wayne, negro, arrested near Quinnimont, charged with the murder of Mrs. John Ailiss, was spirited away to the mountains in the custody of Sheriff D. W. Wiseman and two deputies.

The strategy of the officers, the troops, and the better citiezns, who stood between the trembling negro suspect and inglorious death, has hardly a parallel in its success. Last night Hinton was in darkness, homes were deserted, the city was overrun with the bloodthirsty men clamoring for his life and many are yet unwilling to believe that the object of their fury is beyond them.

After fruitless attempts to rush the prisoner by the mob from the special train on which he had been placed, but which had been disabled, the mob was given to understand that the negro was to be taken back to jail, and up the hill from the station the leaders charged. Meantime the negro, held tremblingly between the sheriff and deputies was told to run for his life towards the east. The mob ran falling over each other to intercept the sheriff. The troops also were covering his retreat.
Wait in Vain.
In vain they waited but the last seen of the negro and his keepers was their disappearing down the track, the retreat guarded by the Fayetteville National Guard. The sheriff and his charge, with two deputies were seen at the town of Avis. There they were lost shight of and last night they were camping in the hills ready when the Charleston guardsmen arrived to be escorted back to the railroad and to safety.
From 2 o'clock in the afternoon when Wayne was brought to the Summers county jail, Hinton was a mob ridden city.
Thomas Wayne was employed at the power house of a coal works near Laurel Creek and was suspected of being the negro who assaulted Mrs. John Alliss, after beating her husband into insensibility. Alliss had said when he recovered sufficiently that he believed the negro looked like a negro at the power house whom he had asked to take his wife and himself to Quinnimont Sunday night on a hand car. He offered him a dollar and the negro refused. En route on foot he was assaulted and left senseless. His wife was ravished and murdered.
Negro Arrested.
With this incident as a clue Officer C. D. Duke, Baldwin officer, and two other officers yesterday arrested the negro. There are rumors here that they found bloody clothing and that the negro declared the clothing belonged to his brother. The negro was placed aboard a train and taken to Hinton, where he was placed in jail. Last night's scenes when 1,000 persons gathered at the false news of arrest were multiplied. Hundreds gathered about the jail and became so threatening that Sheriff Wiseman and his deputies became alarmed. The executive offices at Charleston were notified and meantime the Fayette county company was ordered out, headed by Captain Samuel Walker, but before help came, even though many citizens volunteered, the situation became so alarming that Sheriff Wiseman feared he could no longer hold the fort. Some of the cooler heads counselled for the time and made a bargain with the mob for a consideration of blood and life. It was agreed that Wayne was to be taken to the station from the jail peaceably.

Feeling of Distrust.

That the mob leaders and the citizens and officers distrusted each other was evidenced by developments. The car in which Wayne was placed was attached to an engine and it was intended to make a dash for Charleston or Fayetteville or other place of safety. The mob fearing this had drained the boiler of the engine, cut off air brakes and generally disabled the locomotives. Ailiss was brought to the Pullman where Wayne was a prisoner. First two Hinton colored fellows were brought into the car and in each case Aidill was positive it was the wrong man.

When Wayne scared and trembling was ushered in, Ailiss complained of a headache and said he could not stand the strain longer. "My head, my head," he said and he would not look at the negro.

Sheriff and Prisoner Swim
Two Rivers and Es-
cape Lynching
Party.

TROOPS ON WAY
TO PRINCETON

The Governor Orders Strong
Guard Placed Around
Princeton Jail.
Princeton, Aug. 17.—(Special)—

After swimming two rivers and driving forty miles through the roughest kind of country, the negro accused of murdering and assaulting Mrs. John Aliff at Quinnimont last Sunday in custody of Sheriff Wineman and Deputy Sheriff T. J. Townsley arrived in Princeton at ten o'clock this morning tired and hungry, having had nothing to eat since yesterday morning. The negro was immediately locked up and deputies have been sworn in to guard the jail as Sheriff Wiseman fears the mob at Hinton, on hearing of the lodgement of the negro in the Jail there will board the first train and come to Princeton.

After placing the negro in jail Sheriff Wiseman talked with Governor Glasscock on the long distance telephone and the Governor advised him to put a strong guard around the jail to prevent mob violence. Fatigued and wearied, Sheriff Wiseman told the Governor he would be unable to complete the journey back to Charleston. The Governor instructed Sheriff Ellison of Mercer county to await the arrival of a detachment of troops who have been instructed to move from Hinton to Princeton and with the prisoner accompany them to Charleston.

Blood hounds were taken to the scene of the murder yesterday morning and took up the trail folowing it to the cabin occupied by the negro now under arrest. The premises were thoroughly searched and a shirt with blood stains on the sleeves was found in a bureau drawer. When questioned the negro claimed they were rust stains.

He protests his innocense, but admits he saw Aliff and his wife walking the Chesapeake & Ohio railroad Sunday night. Sheriff Wiseman stated today when the mob had surrounded the Pullman car at Hinton, the negro was not a bit scared, and during the rough ride through the country the negro said he would be able to clear himself of the charge against him.

By a clever ruse Sheriff Wiseman dodged the furious mob at Hinton Monday night and soon had the prisoner concealed in the darkness. After wading Greenbrier river, and swimming across New River Sheriff Wiseman secured a wagon. The prisoner was manacled and placed on his back in the bed of the wagon. Hay was strewn over the negro to hide him and the journey to Princeton was started.

john-wayne-hinton-1910-08-16.A42:
NO INDICTMENT
AGAINST WAYNE
Case Must Await Regular Court Term Which Will Be In October.
No indictment was returned at Fayetteville yesterday against Thomas Wayne, the negro who is held here charged with ravishing and murdering Mrs. John Ailiff. No indictment was returned because there was no grand jury called to investigate the case.

There will be no special grand jury, as the criminal judge of Fayette county is only empowered by law to conduct court at regular stated intervals. The circuit judge of Fayette county has the power to call a special grand jury, but as no special term of the criminal court could be held no time would be saved by a special grand jury.

In view of these facts the case must go over until the next regular term of the Fayette court, which takes place in October.—Huntington Advertiser, Aug. 30.

Excitement Over a Pair of Tramps. Other News Around Marshville.
A great deal of excitement prevailed in Marshville Thursday when two negroes jumped from a freight train and "took to their heels." It was supposed that one of the men was the negro who shot and killed Constable Sing at McFarlan about a week ago. Policeman Ashcraft pursued one of them and fired three shots. Mr. J. E. Bailey heard the shots and ran out and caught the negro. Chase was then made of the other, who escaped after Mr. Ashcraft had taken one shot at him. The negro captured proved to be nothing more than just a stray fellow beating the train.

Clayton, the 4-year-old son of Mr. W. Hamp Griffin of New Salem township, died last Thursday from blood poisoning, which was caused by a stone bruise on one of his feet. Mr. A. T. Marsh died at his home at Hiddenite, Alexander county, last Friday. Mr. Marsh was a native of this county and a brother of Mrs. Mary A. Harrell of this place. He was eighty odd years old and was a good christian gentleman who has lived a life of usefulness. He is survived by a large number of children. Some of our citizens seem to be a

little discouraged over the fact that crops are late. We have been taking notice of the seasons for the past several years and it really does appear to us that they have changed. We have cold weather later in the spring than of former years, and another evidence of the change is that June bugs didn't get here this year until July.

Mr. M. C. Helms of Lanes Creek township has a little plat of land which he has improved until it is showing the real value of fewer acres given more attention. The land is about square and it is 114 yards around it. Off of this patch Mr. Helms has gathered this year: 30 bushels Irish potatoes, 21 bushels onions, and has 8 rows groundpeas and three rows sweet potatoes yet to harvest.
We have heard it remarked several times lately that money is scarcer than usual at this season of the year. We don't know about that, but it is a well known fact that farmers who could conveniently do so paid cash for their fertilizers last spring in order to avoid paying time prices. This perhaps accounts for the little money now in the country. It might also be remembered that a dollar looks bigger during the summer season than at any other time—especially through cider-making months.

Raid Results Fatally. Paleham, Ga., Aug. 1.—One negro is dead, one is dying and two others have bullet wounds as a result of a battle with officers on the outskirts of this place this afternoon. It was reported to the officers that a dozen negroes were gambling in a house there and a half dozen men joined in a raid on the place. When the officers appeared, the negroes opened fire. James Brooks was killed; Charles Boyd was fatally wounded, and the other two negroes shot when the officers returned the fire. Five other negroes were captured, though one wounded negro escaped. No white men were injured. Have Running Fight.
Plqua, O., Aug. 1.—In a pitched battle between policemen and a band of negroes at Bradford today, one of the negroes was fatally shot. The officers approached the negroes and were fired upon. In a running fight, extending over a mile, scores of shots were exchanged between the negroes and pursuing officers.

The negroes surrendererd when one of their number fell mortally wounded.

Will Discus Railroad Law.

Portsmouth, N. H., Aug. 1.—Railroad attorneys representing practically every railroad system in the United States arived here today to attend a conference tomorrow. Colonel Henry L. Stone, general counsel of the Louisville & Nashville system, who summoned the lawyers for the meeting, announced that the purpose of the gathering is to discuss the railroad bill enacted by the last congress and to consider its probable effect upon railroads engaged in interstate traffic. The conference probably will last three days.

Pass Books Will Be Used.

Washington, Aug. 1.—The ancient and long establishing pass book system, used in ordinary savings institutions, will be adopted for the proposed postal savings banks when they are established by the United States Government. The committee of officials that has been perfecting the plans for the postals banks had been considering what is known as the coupon system for postal bank deposits, but has now decided that, while having some advantages, that system might produce complications that would be undesirable.

Will Plend Later.

New York, August 1.—Erwin Wider. the cashier of the Russo-Chinese bank whose speculations in Wall street caused a loss to the bank of something over $500,000, was not forced, as expected, to plead today to the indictment charging him with grand larceny. When Wider appeared in court this afternoon, for aarignment, his counsel asserted that the District Attorney had consented to a brief postponement of the pleading. Judge O'Sullivan of the court of general sessions set next Wednesday.

Catholic Knights Meet.

Quebec, August 1.—The annual convention of Knights of Columbus of America opened here today. Hundreds of delegates from Canada and the United States, New Foundland, Cuba and Panama are in attendance. At the close of the convention on Thursday a pilgrimage to Rome and Genoa will be made. Carrier Pigeon Killed.

Cootapa, Aug. 1.—(Special)—One day last week Mr. Jesse Rushing, mistaking it for a blue-darter hawk, killed a large blue pigeon which proved to have around each leg a neatly fixed aluminum band with the following engraved letters and figures: In right band, "U. S.: 44596," and on left band, "F. R. Z. 550" and a mathematical drawing with the letter J inside. These bands are now in the possession of J. W. McCarty.

Fires Shot Into Heart.

Hattiesburg, Miss., Aug. 1. After writing a letter to her brother, said to live in California, Mrs. Anna Reeves requested her mother to post it late

last night and while alone, fired a revolver shot through her heart, dying instantly. Mrs. Reeves was a stenographer in the local office of a lumber company. Her husband is in the jewelry business in Birmingham, Ala.

Wages Increased.
Franklin, N. H., August 1.—The wages of thousands of paper mill workers in New Hampshire, New York state, Vermont and Maine and Maine chussetts were advanced an average five per cent today by the International Paper Co.

Gets Heav Reprimand.

Washington, Aug. 1.—Lieutenant Commander Henry T. Baker, on duty at the Bremerton Navy Yard, Washington, was today reduced fifty numbers and a public reprimand sent to him by the navy department as the outcome of a conviction by court martial on a charge of uttering a false hod.

Fifteen Drown During Storm.

Fifteen Drown During Storm.

Munich, Bavaria, August 1.—Nine young men and six girls were drowned in the Lake of Traun by the capsizing of a barge in a storm yesterday.

Engineers Get Increase.

Lafayette, Ind., August 1.—Monon railroad engineers were notified today of an advance of from 10 to 20 per cent in wages. The new scale is effective January 1.

TWO NEGROES KILLED EBY POSSE.
Three Dying After Siege of a House in Georgia Town by the Sheriff.
PELHAM, Ga., Aug. 1. In a battle with a Sheriff and posse about 8 o'clock tonight two negroes were killed and three probably fatally wounded.

Late this afternoon Sheriff Shocklev was informed that negroes were causing a disturbance about two miles from Pelham. The Sheriff summoned a posse and went to the scene. He found the negroes, who had learned of the coming of the posse, barricaded in a house.

The posse surrounded the house. The Sheriff ordered them to surrender. The negroes answered by firing on the posse. The posse returned the fire, completely riddling the house with bullets.

After the posse had kept up fire for some time the negroes asked for quarter. When the house was entered two negroes were found dead, three almost dying and four cowering under beds unharmed.

It is said the negroes had gathered at the house to shoot craps.

Since that time one of the wounded, James Brown, has died, and another, Charles Boyd, is in a critical condition. The others will probably recover. At first it was feared that a general riot would take place, but everything has quieted down.

WOMAN FOILS A MOB.
Haits on Her Way to Church, and Pistol in Hand, Defends Negro.
EATON, Ga., July 31. — A mob clamoring for the life of Will Ingram, a negro, was foiled to-day by the bravery of Mrs. Susie Hillhouse of this place, who stood in front of the negro, pistol in hand, and told the mob that there should be no lynching.

The negro, accused of burglary, had been arrested, but broke away from the officer and fled through town pursued by a crowd firing at him. Mrs. Hillhouse was leaving her home for church when the exhausted negro fell at her feet and cried to her to save his life.

He had a pistol, which he gave to Mrs. Hillhouse. She took the weapon and faced the mob as it approached. She asserted it would be a shame to lynch the negro and declared that she would not allow such an outrage on the law.

The courage of Mrs. Hillhouse appealed to the mob, and she was cheered and a promise given that the negro would not be harmed. The leaders of the mob then took the negro and escorted him to jail, Mrs. Hillhouse accompanying to see that the negro was not harmed.

Surrendered to White Woman.
Eatonton Ga. Special—Foiled in
Eatonton, Ga., Special.—Foiled in an attempt to set free all the prisoners in Putnam county jail here, Will Ingram, negro, alleged to be a burglar, Saturday overpowered Deputy Sheriff Ingram Phillips, broke through a cordon of citizens, received bullet in his arm and fled with several hundred persons behind him firing shotguns and pistols.

He was pursued into a residence section of the city and fearing capture and possible death, surrendered to a white woman, throwing his pistol, which he had taken from the deputy sheriff, at her feet. The woman stood in front of him as the crowd of pursuers advanced and begged for the negroe's life so effectually that he was returned to jail without further harm.

D.—The shooting and wounding of a policeman by a negro, the wounding of a special officer and the final killing of the negro by a well-directed shot from the revolver of another policeman, were events which kept the central part of this city in a state of excitement. About a thousand men assisted in the search for the negro after the trouble began, many of them demanding that he be lynched if caught. Pleading on the part of the local officers and cooler heads among the mob prevented an attack being made on the homes of inoffensive negroes.
Chariton Likely to Go Free. Washington.—Porter Chariton, confessed murderer of his wife at Lake Como, Italy, some six weeks ago, is likely to go entirely free of punishment. The time limit within which extradition may be asked for will shortly expire, and it does not now appear probable the Italian government will take the necessary steps to demand of the United States the return of the young man to Italy.

Cut Wire Screen in Tunica Residence and Grabbed Nine-Year-Old Girl, Whose Screams Brought Help.
Tunica, Miss., Aug. 25.—Cutting the wire screen on a bedroom window, Will Jones, a negro, on Monday night reached through the opening and grabbed Laura Thomas, nine years old, the daughter of C. W. Thomas, who lives at Bostick's Mill, six miles Southeast of Tunica.

The child's screams brought her mother, who also clutched the little girl in an effort to prevent her being dragged through the window and for a few minutes the mother and negro tugged for possession of the child.

White men on the place were tracted by the screams of Mrs. Thomas, and the little girl, and their appearance frightened the negro away. Investigation showed that all the negroes on the place except Will Jones were asleep and bloodhounds were secured from Memphis and put on his trail. The negro has been located, and if caught it is feared a synching will follow.

GIRL RESCUED FROM NEGRO Fiend Tried to Pull Little Girl Through Window—Mother Rushes in and Prevents Crime.
Tunica, Miss.—Screaming with terror because a negro had her by the arms and was pulling her from bed through an open window, and begging her mother, who rushed into the room and seized her by the legs, to protect her from the brute, little Laura Thomas, the nine-year-old daughter of C. W. Thomas, had a harrowing experience.

Her screams, coupled with the cries of her mother, quickly assembled the white men in the place and they chased the negro away. Bloodhounds have been on the trail and he has been located.

The little girl retired early and was soon fast asleep. Will Jones, one of the negroes employed by her father, stole up to the house, cut the wire screen on the bedroom window and, reaching through, grabbed the child. Despite her screams the negro held on and clumsily tried to get her through the window, while the mother rushed to her rescue.
